1. Price per square foot
Price per square foot divides a sale price by the living area, so homes of
different sizes can be set side by side. Use it with care: small homes tend to
show a higher figure than large ones in the same street.

2. Keeping houseplants healthy
Most houseplants want bright light that does not scorch their leaves, soil that
dries a little between waterings, and a pot with a hole in the bottom. Yellow
leaves usually point to too much water; crisp brown tips usually point to too
little humidity. Repot in spring, one size up, and feed lightly through the summer.

3. The sale-to-list ratio
The sale-to-list ratio sets what a home sold for against what the seller last
asked. For each closed sale, take the close price over the final list price,
that is ClosePrice divided by ListPrice as it stood when the listing ended, not
OriginalListPrice. Across the sales of a period, report the median of those
per-sale ratios, rounded half to even at three decimals.
A reading of 1.020 says the typical home went for 2% over asking; 1.000 says it
went at asking; 0.975 says it went for 2.5% under asking. Some teams call the
same measure list-to-close or close-to-list; the arithmetic stays the same.
---- page break ----
4. Choosing comparable sales
Comparable sales, or comps, are recent sales of homes much like the one you are
pricing. Good comps sit close by, ideally in the same postal code, and only
widen to the whole city when the postal code has too few. They share the same
kind of home, so a condo is never priced against detached houses, and they are
near in size, a band of about a fifth either side of the subject's floor area.

Recency matters as much as nearness. A six-month window is the usual choice,
and it should be counted back from the date the data runs to rather than from
the calendar on your desk, because a data set that stopped updating a few weeks
ago would otherwise drop its newest sales for no good reason. When the window
holds too few sales, say so plainly instead of stretching it quietly. Seasons
move prices too: spring sales often run a little warmer than winter ones, so a
window that spans both smooths out a swing that a single month would exaggerate.

Before any math, clean the list. Drop sales that closed before their contract
date, sales with prices far too low to be real, homes with a living area under a
couple of hundred square feet, and duplicate records of the same sale, keeping
the latest copy. Each of these is a data error far more often than a real event,
and a single one can drag a small sample well off course.

With a clean list, work out the price per square foot of each sale and take the
median, which a single odd sale cannot pull the way it pulls an average. Show
the spread as well: the middle half of the sales, from the lower quarter mark to
the upper quarter mark, tells a reader how tightly the comps agree. A median
from five sales that agree closely says more than one from twenty that scatter.

Last, compare the subject with that median and state the gap as a whole
percentage above or below. Keep the wording modest. Comps describe what similar
homes sold for; they do not appraise the home, and a reader should hear the
count of sales and the window alongside every figure you give.
---- page break ----
5. Months of supply
Months of supply estimates how long the homes now for sale would take to sell
at the recent pace, with no new ones coming in. Divide the active count by the
number of sales per month. A low figure points to a seller's market.

6. Median or average
A median is the middle value once the figures are sorted, so one mansion in a
street of cottages barely moves it. An average adds every figure and divides,
so that one mansion can lift it a long way. Market reports lean on the median.

7. Kinds of homes
Detached single-family houses, condos, and townhouses sell to different buyers
at different prices per square foot, so a fair comparison keeps each kind apart
and never mixes a condo figure into a house figure.

8. Days on market
Days on market tells you how long a home sat for sale before it found a buyer or
left the market. A short count in a busy area hints that buyers are competing;
a long count hints that the price or the home itself is putting buyers off.
Who listed the home, such as the name in ListAgentFullName, plays no part in it.
Two figures are easy to mix up. One counts only the present listing period; the
cumulative figure adds up every period, so relisting a home does not wipe out
the days it already spent on the market.
